item.title: USDCHF falls on firmer Swiss CPI, but buyers lean against the 100 day MA
item.description:
The USDCHF moved lower during the European session after Swiss inflation came in stronger than expected. October CPI rose 0.2% versus an unchanged reading expected, while annual inflation increased to 1.5% from 1.0%, above the 1.3% forecast. The firmer data supported the CHF and gave USDCHF sellers another push to the downside.

However, the sellers ran into a key technical target. The falling price reached the rising 100 day moving average near 0.81563, just above a swing area between 0.81383 and 0.81513. Buyers leaned against that support and stalled the fall.

Sellers had their shot. Buyers are pushing back.

The move lower followed failures near the 200 hour moving average on Friday and again yesterday. Those failures gave sellers the go-ahead to push lower, with today’s inflation report providing an additional fundamental shove to the downside.

But even with the news on their side, sellers could not sustain momentum through the next major support target. The bounce from the 100 day moving average shows buyers were willing to step in where risk could be defined and limited.

That keeps the buyers in the game. They still have work to do to take more control.

The 0.82162–0.82250 swing area is the next barometer

The rebound has brought the price back toward the familiar swing area between 0.82162 and 0.82250. That zone has acted as both support and resistance on multiple occasions going back to September. The 38.2% retracement of the August-to-October rally also cuts through the area at 0.82243.

I would expect some slowing of the bounce here.

Above that zone, the falling 100 hour moving average at 0.82335 and 200 hour moving average at 0.82447 add another layer of resistance. Buyers need to get and stay above those moving averages to take more of the downside pressure off the pair. If successful, the next swing area comes in between 0.82636 and 0.82740.

What would give sellers more control?

If resistance holds, sellers can look back toward 0.81905–0.81826, followed by the 50% midpoint at 0.81717.

Below that, the 100 day moving average near 0.81563 remains a key downside barometer. Getting below that moving average and through the 0.81383–0.81513 swing area would open the door toward the 61.8% retracement at 0.81191.

For now, buyers have defended support. Sellers have resistance above to lean against.

Education: News provides the push. Technical levels define the risk.

Stronger Swiss inflation gave traders a reason to sell USDCHF. The 100 day moving average gave buyers a place to lean against with close risk.

Holding support can trigger a bounce, but reversing the broader bearish bias requires buyers to reclaim resistance. Watch how the price behaves at the swing area and hourly moving averages. Those tests will help determine whether this is a corrective rebound or the start of a stronger recovery.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOC's Macklem: There could be a need to raise the policy rate further
item.description:
From Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem:

  • There could be a need to raise the policy rate further
  • Will proceed carefully given uncertainties
  • Decisions will be taken one meeting at a time
  • Outlook for inflation has deteriorated
  • Hike needed to reduce risk elevated energy prices become generalized inflation
  • Less scope for monetary accommodation
  • Cost pass-through expected to increase over the next year
  • Growth outlook has improved modestly despite US trade actions
  • Growth likely to slow in Q4 as new US tariffs weigh
  • CPI seen rising to about 3.5% by year-end
  • Inflation to stay at or above 3% through much of 2027
  • Indicators continue to point to some excess supply
  • Uncertainty still elevated on Middle East, Canada-US trade

We heard most of this after the Bank of Canada meeting. He isn't acknowledging some recent weakness in Canadian economic data but he might be pressed on that. The market is divided about the December meeting with a 56% chance of a hike priced in and about 75 bps priced in over the coming year.

He kept the door open to further tightening in his opening statement, saying there “could be a need to raise the policy rate further” after last week’s 25 bp hike to 2.50%, the first increase since July 2023. He tempered that with a pledge to proceed carefully and take decisions one meeting at a time.

The case rests on oil. Persistently high crude and refinery margins have kept CPI near 3% since April, and the BOC sees it climbing to about 3.5% by year-end and staying at or above 3% through much of 2027. Macklem flagged rising cost pass-through from businesses and a recovering economy as reasons the energy shock could become more persistent. Growth is expected to dip in Q4 on new US tariffs before rebounding to about 2% in 2027-28. He still noted some excess supply in the economy, which makes this a hawkish-but-cautious tone rather than a commitment to a hiking cycle.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The broader US stock indices are making a play to the upside. Nasdaq indices bounce from the 200 day MAs
item.description:
The broader US stock indices are moving higher today after both the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 approached their key 200-day moving averages yesterday. Buyers leaned against those technical barometers and stalled the declines. Today, they are getting a bounce.

For the Nasdaq Composite, yesterday’s low reached 25,145.95, just above its rising 200-day moving average near 25,073. The Nasdaq 100 came even closer. Its low of 27,967.44 was only about 15 points above its 200-day moving average, currently at 27,952.83.

Today, the Nasdaq Composite is up 191 points, or 0.76%, while the Nasdaq 100 is up 202 points, or 0.73%. Support has held so far, keeping the buyers in play. The next question is whether they can build on that bounce and push through resistance.

For the Nasdaq Composite, initial resistance comes near 25,570. Above that, the swing level at 25,831.74 becomes the next key target. Yesterday’s high stalled just short of that level before the index rotated lower. Getting above—and staying above—it would give buyers more confidence and strengthen the recovery.

Until those resistance levels are broken, the rebound remains vulnerable to another failed move higher. The buyers have held support. Now they need to show they can take back resistance. If they cannot, attention shifts back toward yesterday’s lows and the key 200-day moving averages below.

For the Nasdaq 100, watch for initial resistance near 28,538. Above that, the swing area between 28,822 and 28,953 becomes the next key upside target. Buyers would need to get above—and stay above—that area to ease the downside pressure and build confidence in the rebound. Until then, sellers can lean against those resistance levels to keep the broader technical bias tilted in their favor

In the video above, I outline the key technical levels for the Nasdaq Composite, Nasdaq 100, and S&P 500. For each index, I define the bias, the risk levels, and the targets that buyers and sellers need to watch. Support has held so far, but what needs to happen next to give buyers more control—and what would put sellers back in the driver’s seat?

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US September factory orders +1.8% vs +1.2% expected
item.description:
• Prior factory orders +0.1%
  • Factory orders excluding transportation +0.5% vs +0.3% prior
  • Durable goods orders revisions +1.9% vs +1.8% prelim
  • Durable goods excluding transportation revisions +0.5% vs +0.5% prelim
  • Durable goods excluding defense +2.3% vs +2.2% prelim
  • Nondefense capital goods orders excluding aircraft +0.6% vs +0.5% prelim

This is a decent report and shows some momentum in factories but it's overshadowed by a jump in the JOLTS number released at the same time. US yields are moving higher in the aftermath of both and USD/JPY is at the highs of the day at 158.37.

For background, the US Census Bureau’s factory orders report, formally the full report on Manufacturers’ Shipments, Inventories and Orders, is released monthly at 10 am ET, about five weeks after the reference month ends. It arrives roughly a week after the advance durable goods report and expands on it by adding nondurable goods.

The headline figure is the monthly change in total new orders for manufactured goods. Nondurables include petroleum and coal products, chemicals, food, paper and plastics. For most nondurable industries, orders are essentially equal to shipments because products aren’t built to order with a backlog. That means swings in oil and commodity prices feed straight into the nondurables figures, since refined petroleum products make up a large share. Markets also look at factory orders excluding transportation, which strips out the volatile aircraft and motor vehicle categories.

The report includes revised durable goods data, which sometimes differ meaningfully from the advance estimates. Economists pay close attention to revisions to core capital goods orders and shipments, nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft. Shipments of those goods feed into the equipment investment component of GDP, and the revised figures can shift growth estimates.

The release also covers manufacturers’ inventories, unfilled orders and the inventory-to-shipments ratio. These offer a read on whether factories are building or drawing down stock and how much work they have in the pipeline.

Because most of the durables data are already known and nondurables largely track commodity prices, factory orders rarely move markets. Its value is in completing the manufacturing picture and providing the revisions that feed into GDP tracking.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: JOLTs Job openings 7.523M vs 7.100M estimate
item.description:
• Prior month 7.079M revised to 7.19M

Details of the JOLTs Job openings: 

  • Job openings: 7.523 million vs 7.190 million, up 333,000.  August revised up by 111,000 to 7.2 million.

  • Job openings rate: 4.5%.

  • Hires: 5.402 million vs 5.271 million, up 131,000.

  • Total separations: 5.319 million vs 5.175 million, up 144,000.

  • Quits: 3.4 million vs 3.0 million in August, revised down by 22,000.

  • Layoffs and discharges: 1.6 million vs 1.8 million in August, revised up by 127,000.

  • Quits rate: 2.1%. Layoffs and discharges rate: 1.0%.

  • Private-sector openings: 6.644 million vs 6.408 million, up 236,000.

  • Government openings: 880,000 vs 782,000, up 98,000.

US job openings were 7.5 million in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That was above August’s upwardly revised 7.2 million, although the BLS characterized the monthly change as little changed. Hiring and total separations also showed little change, pointing to a broadly steady labor market.

The more notable development was the increase in workers voluntarily leaving their jobs. Quits rose to 3.4 million, led by a 197,000 increase in accommodation and food services. That can signal greater confidence in finding another position, although the concentration in one industry tempers the broader message. Quits were up 375,000 from a year earlier.

Job openings increased by 104,000 in state and local government excluding education, while accommodation and food services added 158,000 hires. Layoffs in health care and social assistance declined by 70,000. Overall layoffs were numerically below August’s revised level, but the BLS described the change as little changed.

Where were the job openings?

Professional and business services led the increase in available positions, with openings rising by 106,000 to 1.310 million. State and local government excluding education added another 104,000 openings. Together, those two categories accounted for roughly 63% of the overall monthly increase.

Manufacturing openings increased by 54,000 to 584,000, while construction openings rose by 36,000 to 298,000. Those are encouraging signs of labor demand. However, an available position is only one step. Businesses still need to turn those openings into actual hires.

Hiring tells a more mixed story

Manufacturing illustrates that distinction. Despite the increase in openings, manufacturing hires fell by 34,000 to 313,000. Professional and business services showed a similar divergence: openings increased, but hires declined by 30,000 to 927,000.

Construction was stronger on both measures, with hiring increasing by 49,000 to 356,000. Retail hiring also rose by 40,000 to 704,000.

The biggest hiring increase came from accommodation and food services, where hires rose by 158,000 to 879,000. That increase alone exceeded the economy-wide hiring gain of 131,000, meaning the remaining industries combined recorded a net decline in hiring.

Hospitality shows turnover, rather than a clear hiring surge

Accommodation and food services also recorded a 195,000 increase in separations to 883,000. Departures therefore slightly exceeded hires during September. Combined with the previously reported increase in quits, the figures point to substantial movement between jobs rather than a clear expansion in staffing.

Financial activities offered a softer signal. Openings fell by 19,000 to 364,000, while hires declined by 12,000 to 156,000.

Quick analysis: The stronger openings figure gives the labor-market bulls some support, but hiring provides a more cautious barometer. Employers advertised more positions in several important industries without a matching increase in recruitment. That mixed picture could temper upward pressure on yields and the dollar from the headline openings increase and gives the Fed reason to assess the broader employment data.

What this report measures: The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) distinguishes available jobs from actual hiring and employee departures. Separations include voluntary quits, layoffs and other departures, so an increase does not automatically mean more workers were dismissed. Monthly industry estimates are subject to revision, and numerical changes are not necessarily statistically significant.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tough to buy into the Iran headlines in the context of the election
item.description:
There are more headlines crossing suggesting positive developments in Iran-US talks, with Al-Arabiya now carrying similar headlines to the earlier ones that weighed on oil.

In contrast, here is Iran security chief Mohsen Rezaei just now:

America's response to Iran's rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them; only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.

Those are the same seven conditions they have been talking about forever and were mostly in the 14-point MOU agreed in June.

The problem is analyzing deal prospects is the calendar. It's in the Trump admin's interest to leak positive Iran headlines this week in order to drive down the price of oil. Perhaps that's too little, too late but it's a reason for skeptcism. You also have lines around negotiating that are very far apart, though obviously there are real efforts at mediation.

Oil has been rebounding on that same skepticism and the latest comments from Rezaei and is now close to flat.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin sellers had their shot and missed. Now it is the buyers’ turn.
item.description:
Sellers could not deliver the downside break

The bitcoin sellers had their opportunity to take more control. On Friday, Monday and again today, the price traded to (and even below today) its 100 day moving average, currently at $76,654 (purple MA line). Those breaks opened the door for a move toward the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the July low at $76,052 and the highlighted swing area extending down toward $74,925.

Those were the targets to get to — and through — if the sellers were going to extend the downside.

They missed.

The price could not sustain a break below the 38.2% retracement, and the swing area that has attracted buyers and sellers since August held. The sellers got below the 100 day MA today briefly, but they could not turn that break into a sustained move lower.

That failure gives buyers a reason to lean against support, define their risk and push back higher. And they did just that today.  

Buyers have their opening, but need to follow through

Now it is the buyers’ turn. However, holding support is only part of the job. They also need to break resistance in their own upward direction.  .

The first upside barometer is the 100 hour moving average near $77,408 on the chart. With the price extending to $77,736, bitcoin buyers are testing that level. Getting above is one step. Staying above and building momentum is the next.

Above that, the falling 200 hour moving average comes in near $78,730. That is the next key hurdle, followed by resistance near $79,146 (prior lows).

Get and stay above those levels, and the buyers would take back more control. The next upside target would then come in near $81,930.

Until those breaks happen, the rebound remains a recovery within the recent move lower. The buyers have their opportunity, but they need to show they can do more with it than the sellers did with theirs.

What would give sellers another chance?

If the rebound stalls against the hourly moving averages, the sellers remain in the game.

A move back below the 100 day MA at $76,656 would weaken the buyers’ progress and put the $76,052 retracement back in play. Below that, the lower edge of the swing area near $74,925 becomes the next key target.

A sustained break below that area would give the sellers the follow-through they have so far failed to deliver. It would also open the door toward the 200 day moving average near $73,158 and the 50% midpoint at $72,554.

For now, however, support held. The focus shifts to whether buyers can turn that successful defense into a break of resistance.

Education: A failed break creates an opportunity, not a guarantee

When the price breaks a key technical level, traders look for momentum in the direction of the break. If that momentum does not develop and the price moves back across the level, the failure becomes information.

In this case, sellers broke below the 100 day MA but could not get through the retracement and swing support below it. That tells us buyers were willing to step in against a defined area.

The next test is whether those buyers can take out resistance. Support defines the risk. The hourly moving averages measure their progress. A move above those averages strengthens the bullish bias; a rejection gives sellers another opportunity.

The lesson is to let the price action confirm the shift. A failed downside break gives buyers an opening, but getting and staying above resistance is what turns that opening into greater control.

In this video

In this video, I show where the bitcoin sellers had their shot below the 100 day moving average, why their failure to break the 38.2% retracement and swing area matters, and what the buyers need to do next. I outline the key barometers, risk levels and upside targets that will help determine which side takes control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: How markets price geopolitical risk: Why de-escalation headlines can trigger major market moves
item.description:
Geopolitical events can have a significant impact on financial markets, especially when they threaten global energy supplies, trade routes or economic stability. Markets constantly assess the potential economic consequences, assign probabilities to different outcomes and adjust asset prices accordingly.

This is why financial markets can rally sharply on the first signs of de-escalation, even when a conflict remains unresolved. Markets may move just based on expectations of a less negative scenario rathen than pricing in peace, for example. 

One of the most important concepts is that markets are forward-looking. Traders are constantly trying to anticipate what might happen over the next 6–12 months rather than caring about current conditions, because the present is already priced in. 

When geopolitical tensions escalate, markets begin to price in the potential economic consequences. These might include supply disruptions, higher energy prices, increased inflation, weaker economic growth and tighter financial conditions. These risks start to get incorporated into prices before the worst-case scenario actually materialises.

For example, when tensions threaten the Strait of Hormuz, oil markets may start pricing in the possibility of supply disruptions even if no barrels have been physically removed from the market. The price increase reflects the additional risk of a future supply shock.

The same mechanism works in reverse. When negotiations progress or the probability of military escalation decreases, markets can quickly remove part of that risk premium. This is why markets sometimes rally on diplomatic headlines even without a concrete agreement.

A risk premium is the additional compensation investors demand for holding an asset exposed to a particular risk. During geopolitical crises, this premium can increase across several asset classes, although the transmission mechanism differs.

Oil: The supply disruption premium

Crude oil is the most directly affected asset during geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East, especially when major producers or strategic shipping routes are affected. When tensions threaten energy infrastructure or important chokepoints, traders begin pricing in the possibility of reduced supply. This pushes oil prices higher even before actual disruptions occur.

The Strait of Hormuz is a good example. A prolonged disruption restricts a significant portion of global oil flows, forcing buyers to compete for alternative supplies and increasing the risk of a global energy shock. However, if diplomatic progress reduces the probability of prolonged disruption, the premium can be unwound. This is why oil prices fall sharply on de-escalation headlines, even before shipping flows fully normalise.

Gold: The safe-haven premium

Gold tends to benefit from geopolitical uncertainty when investors seek protection against unpredictable events and potential financial market instability. However, this is not always true, as we've seen this year during the US-Iran war. In fact, higher energy prices can increase inflation expectations and push bond yields higher, supporting the US dollar and real interest rates. These developments can offset gold's safe-haven demand.

Gold is better supported during geopolitical tensions when the Federal Reserve can look through the short-term impact of higher energy prices. When inflation is not a problem, gold generally finds support as Treasury yields fall on safe-haven demand. It's never just black and white in the markets.

Bonds: The inflation and growth trade-off

Geopolitical conflicts can create opposing forces for bonds. On one side, traders may seek the safety of government bonds during periods of heightened uncertainty. This increases demand and pushes yields lower. On the other side, conflicts that threaten energy supplies can drive inflation expectations higher. If traders believe central banks will need to maintain tighter monetary policy, bond yields can rise.

The growth implications matter too. If higher energy prices threaten economic activity, markets may start pricing in weaker growth and eventually lower interest rates. Therefore, the direction of bond yields depends on which forces dominate the economic context.

Equities: The growth and earnings premium

Equity markets are exposed to geopolitical risks through several channels. Higher energy prices increase costs for businesses and consumers, potentially reducing corporate margins and household spending. Uncertainty can also delay investment decisions, weaken confidence and increase the cost of capital. As a result, traders may revise their expectations for corporate profitability and sell stocks, especially when valuations are high.

When tensions ease, the opposite can happen. Lower energy prices improve the growth outlook, reduce inflation concerns and lead to less hawkish monetary policy expectations. This combination can support both economic growth and corporate earnings expectations, creating the conditions for a rally as markets reprice the prior negative outlook.

In conclusion, markets constantly price and reprice expectations, which is why the biggest moves often occur when new information changes the perceived likelihood of escalation or de-escalation. Understanding what is already priced in and waiting for a catalyst that changes the picture is key. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Never tell me the odds: Prediction markets see Democrats taking control of House and Senate
item.description:
Prediction markets are pointing to a Democratic sweep of Congress in today's US midterm elections, with the odds of Democrats taking control of the Senate rising sharply in recent weeks.

As of around 8 am ET on Tuesday, November 3, the latest prices from Kalshi and Polymarket show:

  • House control: Democrats 94–95%, Republicans 6–7%

  • Senate control: Democrats 78%, Republicans 23–24%

The Senate race has seen the biggest shift. Kalshi had Democratic control priced at 74% at midday Monday, up from 63% in early October and 44% in March.

Here are the latest approximate Kalshi prices for some of the key Senate races:

Kansas is the one that would be the big shocker. This is Mitch McConnell's old seat, which he last won in 2020 by a margin of 57.76% to 38.23%. The odds flipped just in the past week.

I'm skeptical of that on but there have been some ghastly polls for Republicans lately. Of course, we've seen this playbook before with some pollsters calling the end of Trumpism on the eve of the 2024 election only for him to win big.

Other notable races include North Carolina, where Democrat Roy Cooper is priced at 97%, and Georgia, where Democratic incumbent Jon Ossoff is at 96%.

Republicans currently hold a 53–47 advantage in the Senate, meaning Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure outright control. As a crosscheck, UK bookmakers have about the same 75-78% odds of Democrats controlling the Senate.

The House market is considerably more one-sided, with Democrats trading near 95% to regain control. 

Nate Silver’s model gives Democrats 82% for the Senate and 96% for the House. Poliwave has Democrats at 85% for the Senate.

The first meaningful clues should arrive around 7:15–8:00 pm ET tonight, with a much clearer picture by 9–10 pm. The earliest races to watch are in Kentucky, Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina and Ohio.

Focus on two things: the Democratic margin relative to the 2024 presidential electionin early-reporting House districts, and whether Republicans are outperforming or underperforming expectations in the Senate races.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Election uncertainty, Iran tensions and rising yields frame the session
item.description:
The balance of power is up for grabs as US voters head to the polls for the midterm elections. For traders, however, the election outcome is an after-the-close event. The North American session will first have to navigate rising Treasury yields, mixed stock futures, US economic data and a Middle East situation that continues to swing between diplomatic optimism and military escalation.

The US dollar is mixed in the morning snapshot. The greenback is higher against the Australian dollar, Swiss franc, Japanese yen and euro, but lower against the New Zealand dollar, Canadian dollar and, marginally, the British pound.

Meanwhile, crude oil is recovering some ground after Monday’s sharp decline, while gold and silver are lower. The message across markets is mixed. There is still hope for a diplomatic breakthrough, but traders continue to face conflicting headlines and unresolved risks.

Middle East: Negotiations continue, but military action clouds the outlook

Yesterday’s hopes for progress toward a US-Iran agreement have been tempered by overnight developments. InvestingLive reported that talks involving Qatari mediators ended without a breakthrough, although contacts between Washington and Tehran continue through intermediaries.

Iran’s proposal links reopening the Strait of Hormuz to relief from the US blockade and restrictions on Iranian oil sales. The gap between continued negotiations and an agreement that can actually be implemented remains important for traders.

Adding to the uncertainty, the Associated Press reported, citing a US official, that the United States carried out strikes against Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz in response to surface-to-air missile threats against US forces. That leaves diplomacy and military pressure operating alongside each other.

For markets, the distinction matters. An agreement that restores shipping and reduces supply risks would give oil sellers more confidence. Further military action could quickly rebuild the geopolitical premium. The next headline still has the potential to change the near-term tone.

US election: The balance of power is the main event after the close

Control of Congress will help determine how much room President Trump has to advance his legislative agenda over the next two years.

A Republican hold of both chambers would preserve a clearer path for legislation. Democratic control of either chamber would increase the need for negotiation over spending and major policy changes. Control of the Senate also matters for appointments and confirmations.

For traders, the implications run through taxes, spending, regulation and government borrowing. The size of the majorities will matter alongside which party wins.

Results will begin taking shape after the stock market closes, and close races could leave control unresolved beyond tonight. That makes the overnight reaction and Wednesday’s opening levels important reference points.

For a preview of the key swing races, see my post: US election: The key races that could tip control of Congress.

RBA raises rates, but AUDUSD moves lower

The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85%, as expected. The decision was made by a 6–3 vote, with three members favoring a pause.

The inflation message was uncomfortable. The RBA revised its inflation outlook materially higher, pointing to domestic capacity pressures, elevated energy prices and the risk that higher inflation expectations become entrenched.

Governor Michele Bullock said growth needs to remain subdued and unemployment needs to rise further to bring inflation down. However, she did not commit to another hike, suggesting it was probably appropriate to wait and assess incoming data.

The AUDUSD is nevertheless down 0.26% at 0.6978 in the supplied snapshot. An expected rate hike does not automatically translate into a stronger currency. Traders also have to assess what comes next and what tighter policy means for growth.

The USD: Mixed, with gains against AUD, CHF and JPY

The dollar’s largest gain among the supplied pairs is against the Australian dollar helped by the rate hike. It is also higher against the Swiss franc and Japanese yen.

The New Zealand dollar shows the strongest percentage gain against the USD in the snapshot, followed by the Canadian dollar. Sterling is little changed.

The current levels are:

  • EURUSD: 1.1177, down 0.07%.

  • USDJPY: 158.22, up 0.18%.

  • GBPUSD: 1.3406, up 0.01%.

  • USDCHF: 0.8202, up 0.22%.

  • USDCAD: 1.3979, down 0.05%.

  • AUDUSD: 0.6978, down 0.26%.

  • NZDUSD: 0.5620, up 0.09%.

Currency ranges: Most pairs still have room to extend

Using the highs and lows in the currency-price snapshot and the 22-day average ranges in the supplied range monitor:

  • EURUSD: 1.1176 to 1.1206 — 30 pips, or 43% of its 69-pip average.

  • GBPUSD: 1.3397 to 1.3429 — 32 pips, or 42% of its 77-pip average.

  • USDJPY: 157.76 to 158.30 — 54 pips, or 108% of its 50-pip average.

  • USDCHF: 0.8150 to 0.8203 — 53 pips, or 84% of its 63-pip average.

  • USDCAD: 1.3951 to 1.3996 — 45 pips, or 104% of its 43-pip average.

  • AUDUSD: 0.6962 to 0.7003 — 41 pips, or 95% of its 43-pip average.

  • NZDUSD: 0.5603 to 0.5631 — 28 pips, or 67% of its 42-pip average.

EURUSD and GBPUSD have the most meaningful room to extend relative to their normal daily movement. Both have completed less than half their average range.

USDJPY and USDCAD have already exceeded their averages, while AUDUSD is close to a normal full-day range. That does not prevent further movement, but those pairs have already covered more ground.

The average range is a barometer, not a ceiling. A data surprise or headline can still stretch a market beyond its normal movement.

US stock futures: Nasdaq higher, Dow lower

The supplied futures figures point to a mixed opening:

  • Dow industrial average futures: down 350 points.

  • Nasdaq 100 futures: up 72 points.

  • S&P is trading above and below unchanged

The divergence keeps the focus on whether strength can broaden as the session develops. With election results still ahead, an early move will need follow-through before traders can have more confidence in the direction.

Treasury yields move higher

US yields are higher across the key maturities:

  • 2-year: 4.608%, up 2.5 basis points.

  • 5-year: 4.7268%, up 3.38 basis points.

  • 10-year: 4.929%, up 3.5 basis points.

  • 30-year: 5.2996%, up 3.06 basis points.

item.title: Squeezing the Lemon: Why Brokers' Growth Is Already in Their Systems
item.description:
On November 24, Alex Piliavsky joins the panel "Your Broker's Growth Is Elsewhere: Ahead of 2027" on the Craft Stage at Old Billingsgate. He plans to argue that it isn't elsewhere at all. Piliavsky began his career at Seperia and went on to hold senior marketing roles, including several C-level positions, at healthtech and fintech companies before co-founding Alchemy Avenue, a lifecycle marketing agency based in Nicosia. Here's a preview of what he'll tell the room.

The panel says growth is elsewhere. You think it's already inside the broker?

Yes. Brokers have already paid for it. Every registration, every verified account, every trader who deposited once and drifted off is sitting in their CRM right now. Most brokers don't squeeze that lemon hard enough. And honestly, a lot of them don't know how to squeeze it. They don't have a clear strategy, the right sequences or the tools to run them. So the default answer becomes buying more traffic.

You've built your methodology around trader psychology. What does that mean in practice?

It means starting from how people actually behave, not from a campaign calendar. Attention spans are short now, for traders as much as anyone. You get a few seconds to make a message worth reading. So every message in a sequence should do one job: move the person one step forward, in as few words as possible, at the moment they're most likely to act.

What that person needs also changes along the way. Someone who just registered is curious but unsure. Someone who just closed their first trade wants to know whether they did it right. Someone who hasn't logged in for a month needs a reason to come back, and a reminder that their account is waiting isn't one.

Where does personalization fit in?

It's the practical side of the psychology. Personalization isn't a first name in the subject line. It's a message that reacts to what the trader did: the instruments they trade, the hours they usually log in, the step where they stopped. Someone who trades gold shouldn't get a promotion on EUR/USD. Most brokers already hold this data across their CRM and trading platform. It just rarely makes it into the messages.

And gamification?

Trading is competitive by nature, and people respond to progress and a bit of chance. Onboarding works better when it's built as steps with visible progress, so finishing it feels like getting somewhere. Raffles give people a reason to come back regularly, which is often exactly what the trader who went quiet a month ago needs. Trading tournaments speak to active traders, because a leaderboard gives a routine session something to win. All of it works for the same reason short messages do. The goal is clear and the next step is always visible.

What should brokers do before they plan 2027?

Put their numbers side by side: registrations, verified accounts, first deposits, second deposits, active traders. Most brokers watch the first two drops closely. The ones after the first deposit get far less attention, and that's where most of the value sits. Then look at each drop and ask what would move more people to the next step. Which message, sent when, on which channel, with which mechanic. Answering that is where the work is, and it's what we've done with many brokers, one conversion step at a time. The growth is already in their systems. The lemon is already in their hands. Most brokers just haven't squeezed it yet.

Alex Piliavsky speaks on "Your Broker's Growth Is Elsewhere: Ahead of 2027" on November 24, from 11:20 to 11:50 a.m., on the Craft Stage at Old Billingsgate. He and fellow Alchemy Avenue co-founder Ohad Galitz will both be at the summit. Book time with them here.

item.title: The S&P 500 stays on the back foot amid geopolitical uncertainty as US midterm elections loom. What's next?
item.description:
The S&P 500 sold off sharply last week as weakness in technology and AI-related stocks weighed on the index. Concerns about the profitability of massive AI investments, disappointing corporate earnings and rising financing costs triggered a rotation away from growth stocks, while increasing uncertainty around future AI spending raised questions about the sustainability of the current earnings and growth outlook.

However, the weakness was led by a broader combination of negative macroeconomic, geopolitical and positioning risks. Higher-than-expected inflation data strengthened concerns about a prolonged tightening cycle from the Federal Reserve, while renewed US-Iran tensions and surging oil prices increased the risk of a growth slowdown. This came at a time when positioning had become very crowded, leaving equities vulnerable to a sharper correction.

Looking ahead, the focus will be on US-Iran negotiations and the US midterm elections. The S&P 500 rebounded yesterday after Iran proposed a two-day framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for US concessions and Iran’s President said that the Supreme Leader had granted the government additional authority regarding negotiations which was taken as a positive sign for greater flexibility to reach a deal.

The market couldn’t sustain the gains, though, and eventually dropped to new lows after the US struck sites on Iran’s Qeshm Island overnight. US officials said the strikes were in response to Iran firing at a US aircraft and did not signal the start of a broader military operation.

Trump said he was not looking to strike Iran after the midterm elections, although officials confirmed that all options remain on the table. Meanwhile, Axios reported that the CIA Director had advised Trump to maintain a "no war, no deal" approach, allowing economic pressure on Iran to continue.

Nevertheless, the negotiations continue with Qatar’s Foreign Ministry Spokesperson saying this morning that both sides are currently studying the proposal and they remain committed to the mediation process.

A breakthrough could trigger a strong relief rally as lower energy prices would ease inflation concerns, reduce expectations of further Fed tightening and improve the growth outlook. Setbacks or renewed military escalation, on the other hand, could trigger another leg lower in equities.

Moving on to US midterm elections, a Democratic takeover of the House is largely expected and should therefore be priced in. A blue sweep could put additional pressure on equities on expectations of greater fiscal restraint, especially without an end to the Iran war. A surprising Republican sweep, on the other hand, could support stocks through expectations of further fiscal expansion.

item.title: Three warning signs the tech selloff isn't over as Wall Street sentiment hangs by a thread
item.description:
It's not the first time this year that Wall Street is being put in a position with its back against the wall this year. But somehow, there is a different air of vulnerability to the latest selloff in tech shares than before this. In previous times, strong earnings was what came to the rescue for investors. This time around, it seems to be the case that even solid earnings isn't enough anymore as AI spending fears are taking over.

After the brutal selloff in October, dip buyers are desperately looking for a reason to put their toes back into the water. But as the market mood feels more fragile by the day, every disappointing earnings report or fresh AI spending concern is threatening to send investors running for the exits.

And looking beneath the surface, there are warning signs that could suggest that the worst may not be over.

Firstly, there is the fact that one of the core components of the AI rally is still taking a very heavy beating. Semiconductor stocks have been slumping hard in the past month and there's still no reprieve in recent sessions.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slumped by 7.2% on Friday, with the selling continuing into Monday this week. That's hardly encouraging when you consider the fact that chipmakers have been the backbone of the AI rally.

Intel's disappointing outlook may have been the one to spark the latest rout, but the weakness has spread to the likes of Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom. So until chip stocks find their feet, I'd be wary of trusting any meaningful Nasdaq recovery.

Secondly, there is the growing concern that Wall Street is losing patience with the whole AI spending bonanza. Amazon, Alphabet and Meta are continuing to pour enormous sums into AI infrastructure but investors seem to have about enough of that. Now, they are questioning more than ever as to when those investments will actually pay off.

Consider this, Amazon's trailing 12-month free cash flow swung to negative $42.4 billion. That's quite the price tag for chasing the AI dream.

Now, the issue here isn't necessarily weak demand. It is simply the fact that spending is accelerating faster than investors are comfortable with, raising uncomfortable questions about returns on investment.

And thirdly, the market breadth isn't offering much reassurance either. As of Monday's close, only about 36% of Nasdaq-listed stocks were trading above their 50-day moving averages. That's a very fragile foundation in trying to argue for a sustained recovery.

Now, the broader S&P 500 is holding up better with roughly two-thirds of its constituents above that same threshold. So, we're still very much looking at a concentrated tech problem rather than any major outright market capitulation. That being said, the signs aren't great especially if this keeps up for longer and threatens a spillover to broader stock sectors.

The next test now will be defined as a battle on multiple fronts. It will be a question of whether chipmakers can stabilise, whether AI spending fears will ease, and whether more stocks in the Nasdaq can join in on any recovery prospects.

So until we see better developments on all those fronts, I wouldn't want to mistake any bounce for a clean bill of health in the market. If anything, the signs above are pointing to the fact that it may not take much to trigger yet another round of selling on Wall Street.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Swiss inflation surprises higher in October but core prices offer some relief
item.description:
• Switzerland October CPI +1.5% vs +1.3% y/y expected
  • Prior +1.0%
  • Switzerland October core CPI +0.5% y/y
  • Prior +0.5%

Swiss headline annual inflation picks up at the start of the third quarter, rising to 1.5% from 1.0% previously. Much like elsewhere around the region, higher energy prices are the main culprit in continuing to feed through to consumer prices. As such, the inflation numbers may look to be heating up again at first glance.

But in looking to core annual inflation, that remains unchanged at just 0.5%. That tells us that the broader inflation picture isn't quite as alarming as the headline reading might suggest.

And for the SNB, that is the most crucial takeaway here. The central bank has been arguing for months that higher energy costs are largely responsible for the inflation pickup, with limited evidence of second-round effects spilling over to the wider economy.

The latest figures we're seeing today doesn't really challenge that narrative as such.

Naturally, headline inflation moving closer to the 2% mark does mean that policymakers won't be entirely comfortable if energy prices continue to stay elevated. That will especially be the case if there is more evidence of businesses eventually passing those higher costs on to consumers.

But at least for now, the SNB still has room to sit comfortably on the sidelines and assess how persistent these inflation pressures might become. In other words, there's no reason to panic just yet.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US-Iran deal still out of reach despite fresh diplomatic hopes ahead of US midterms
item.description:
And round and round we go. We started the week with renewed optimism that the US and Iran might finally be inching towards a diplomatic breakthrough. That led to oil prices tumbling on Monday as hopes of a potential deal gathered momentum. But fast forward to today, and we're pretty much back where we started.

Anyone got a case of déjà vu? These have been the same sort of headlines that we have been dealing with for almost seven months now.

The latest comments from a senior Iranian official to Reuters:

  • Tehran's conditions must be met if the US wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened, with nuclear talks only possible afterwards
  • Iran is prepared to respond forcefully to US strikes, both in the region and beyond
  • Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington

Now, that is hardly the language of two sides getting ready to shake hands.

The thing about all this is that the sticking point remains the same. Iran wants its demands addressed before reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while the US is not willing to agree to those terms. And despite the diplomatic exchanges, neither side appears ready to make the concessions needed to break the deadlock.

For markets, it just exemplifies the narrative that the underlying geopolitical risks haven't gone anywhere.

While Monday's selloff in the oil market may have shown how quickly traders were willing to price in a potential easing of tensions, the fact of the matter is the reality is not quite there yet.

There's been a lot of talk about what could happen once the US midterms are over and done with. So, we'll have to see if Trump will be bold enough to step up his game after the election later today. The real test will come after the votes are cast, when we'll see whether diplomacy can produce anything concrete or whether the threat of renewed military escalation returns to the forefront. Knowing Trump as we do, the latter certainly seems rather likely.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: FX option expiries for 3 November 10am New York cut
item.description:
There is just one key expiry level to take note of on the day, as highlighted in bold below.

That being for EUR/USD at the 1.1200 level, which sits less than 10 pips away from the spot price. The expiries could help anchor price action around the figure level into the cut, should there be no major headlines to jolt the pair before we get to the US midterms later.

The pair has been struggling to hold any pushes above 1.1200 in recent days, so the expiries will add another layer for buyers to chew through in order to establish a more convincing upside push.

But all else being equal, we could see price action be more contained closer to the figure level with the expiries acting more as a magnet for the session ahead.

As for overall trading sentiment, the dollar will be a main focus today with the US midterm elections in focus. That alongside the broader risk mood will be key drivers for how traders will react in the day ahead, before we slowly switch back to focus on the upcoming US jobs report on Friday.
